title: Five Cocktails From the Best New Bars of 2026
summary: These are the must-try cocktails from our favorite openings, from a Puerto Rican highball to a Malört-like aperitif.
content:
It’s time to raise a glass to the Best New Bars of 2026. For a taste of the most innovative, exciting openings of the past year, make these cocktails from our awardees.

At Peach Crease Club in Denver, co-owners Alex Jump and Stuart Jensen take inspiration from dishes around the world, from borscht to buko salad. Nonalcoholic drinks have been thoughtfully considered here—fitting, given Jump’s advocacy with the organization Focus on Health. Made with The Pathfinder (an N/A amaro) and Three Spirit Nightcap, this fully spirit-free recipe pays homage to the Southern pairing of peanuts and Coca-Cola (sometimes called farmer’s Coke). To carbonate the cocktail, Peach Crease Club uses a NitroPress, but at home, you can top the mix with club soda.

title: Ten Years Later, the Spinzall Keeps Spinning
summary: The first appliance specifically designed for bartenders continues to influence how cocktails are made around the world.
content:
This article appears in Pre Shift, our newsletter for bartenders and the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more stories like this in your inbox. 

To someone who’s never bartended, Josh Seaburg’s Spinzall tattoo might easily be mistaken for a food processor. But to Seaburg, the tattoo, which has the words “All I Do Is Spin” emblazoned in block letters across his right calf, is a testament not only to his love of bartending but also his affection for Dave Arnold’s groundbreaking desktop centrifuge, which he’s owned since its inception. “Instead of bringing in a photo of it for my tattoo artist, I brought the actual Spinzall into the shop,” he says.

Seaburg manages two cocktail bars in Norfolk, Virginia, and was among the earliest adopters of the Spinzall. As the tattoo suggests, he remains a persistent evangelist for the device’s utility behind the bar, having originally purchased one through Arnold’s Kickstarter campaign, which launched 10 years ago this month, for the promotional price of $699. (Upon official release, the Spinzall retailed for $999.) “I’d already been following Dave’s Cooking Issues blog and listening to his podcast for years,” says Seaburg, “so by the time the Spinzall hit my bar, I was already pretty well-versed in all of the ins and outs of clarification.” 

Josh Seaburg’s Spinzall tattoo.

Over the past decade, trends in the bar industry have come and gone, but the Spinzall has remained a stalwart in the prep kitchens of top bars around the world. More so than perhaps any other bar-centric innovation, it continues to influence how a generation of modern bartenders approaches making cocktails.

Long before Arnold opened his first bar Booker and Dax in 2012, he’d already been experimenting with commercial-grade centrifuges. As the director of culinary technology at the French Culinary Institute in New York City in the early 2000s, Arnold spent thousands of hours testing equipment, including rotary evaporators and immersion circulators, to gauge their utility for chefs. At the time, he was obsessed with clarifying lime juice to perfect the Gin & Tonic.

“Back then, there were a handful of chefs using centrifuges in Spain, but no one was really using them here in the U.S,” he says. “So, when Unilever donated a super-speed centrifuge the size of a washing machine to the institute, lime juice was one of the first things I tested on it.” To force-carbonate the combined ingredients in a proper G&T, he had determined that the lime juice needed to be crystal clear. But popular clarification techniques at the time, such as using agar agar or the freeze-thaw method, weren’t effective with lime juice, which has a low pH and oxidizes quickly.

Arnold eventually perfected a method for clarifying lime juice in a centrifuge using enzymes and wine fining agents, which he wrote about at length in his seminal 2014 book Liquid Intelligence. But the technology wasn’t readily available to most bars because commercial centrifuges were prohibitively expensive—laboratory-grade models could cost upwards of $60,000.

“I realized that if you build a bar program around something that you can only afford to have one of and it breaks, you’re toast,” says Arnold. “So, I thought, what the bar community needed was something small and cheap enough that they could have several of them. They needed to be portable, safe and able to deliver the same results as a $10,000 bench-top machine, without the need for advanced training or expertise.”

title: Crab Rangoon Olives, Anyone?
summary: For your next Martini, holiday party or DIY gift, here are five snacks-turned-garnishes to make this season.
content:
You can make a Martini in all manner of ways now: up in a highball; washed with mochi rice; even infused with saffron, if you’re fancy. But for all of the attention that’s paid to riffing on the drink and to finding the perfect gin (or vodka) for the cocktail, there is sometimes a lack of focus on the olives in the glass —if, after all, you are an olive-over-twist person. Not anymore; a few bars across the country are paying special attention to the garnish. The below recipes are worth throwing together this holiday season, whether you plop them into your coupe or simply snack on them at aperitivo hour (we know not everyone loves a fancy olive in their drink). Use these as inspiration for your holiday entertaining—or DIY gifting—needs.

“I am from Mexico City, and every time I go to Mexico with [chef] Jeremiah [Stone], he becomes obsessed with a certain ingredient or preparation,” says Fabian Von Hauske of New York City’s Bar Contra and Wildair. Right now, “he loves chamoy.” Von Hauske says the floral and fatty notes of Castelvetrano olives harmonize well with the spicy-sweet flavors of chamoy. His version of the condiment “is not a traditional one, but we use a lot of ingredients we tend to use in the drinks or on other dishes at the restaurant,” like umeboshi and acid powders. These olives are served as a snack, but we wouldn’t mind them in a Mexican Martini.

title: This Thanksgiving, Don’t Use AI to Pick Your Wines. Use Somm Intelligence.
summary: A new project empowers curious holiday drinkers to ask real experts for their advice.
content:
“Last week, I watched the episode of The West Wing where President Bartlet calls the Butterball hotline and is arguing with them,” says Evan Roscoe, a Napa, California-based social media consultant for wineries. “I thought, ‘This would be a really great thing for the wine industry.’”

Over Halloween, while trick-or-treating with his kid, Roscoe kept thinking about it. He’d also learned that search traffic about wine surges before Thanksgiving. He came up with a plan: a website, with a chat, not unlike the many chatbots popping up these days, but powered by humans with real wine expertise answering real questions. It would run for 24 hours, the day before Thanksgiving, and invite anyone to ask any question they have about buying, selecting, or pairing bottles for the holiday. “Lord knows we like to talk about our wine,” he says, “and this is the time that people have questions.”

Before going to bed on Saturday, Roscoe posted an Instagram story mapping out the idea with a poll asking if people were interested in helping. “I think the options were, ‘Yes, I want to make wine fun’ or ‘No, I’ll already be drunk,’” he says. When he woke up, he had 50 interested wine industry experts. He launched Ask Wines on Monday, jokingly describing it as being fueled by somm—rather than artificial—intelligence. So far, the experts interested comprise sommeliers, winemakers, wine directors, wine buyers, drinks writers and people pursuing WSET diplomas. The author and content creator André Mack will be answering questions, as will Megan Bell, who founded Margins Wine and now works for the California Association of Winegrape Growers. 

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Evan Roscoe (@evan__roscoe)

Finding so many people willing to lend a hand wasn’t all that surprising. “Wine is seen as unapproachable, but wineries and people who work in wine are very approachable,” says Roscoe. That’s also the basis of the project. “I think that when people are asking questions about wine, it isn’t necessarily a lot of how-to’s. It’s more of a reassurance that they’re not violating some unspoken rule.” Because of that, he anticipates that a lot of the questions coming into the chat will be about what pairings people are “allowed” to have, or how many bottles to pick up for a certain number of people, or “I’m at the grocery store and there are a thousand options. What do I pick?” 

Roscoe’s project comes at a time when apparently customers keep turning to bots rather than the professional wine experts who are there to personally advise them. The reasons for this trend have been enumerated: People may feel overwhelmed with the amount of options or insecure about a lack of wine knowledge or they might not know what the role of the sommelier really is (or, cynically, maybe they are addicted to asking the robot in their phones for information). Part of Roscoe’s aim is to show those people that most of the wine industry really does want to help. Wine, he points out, doesn’t have to be pretentious.

“This is a success to me if people walk away thinking that talking to people in the wine industry is a lot easier than they thought,” he says. “The whole point is that we can connect with wine drinkers and help them have a better holiday.”

title: Our Favorite Stirred Tequila Cocktails
summary: There’s more to the spirit than Margaritas and Palomas. Here are some of our favorite ways to use it in fall- and winter-ready drinks.
content:
While tequila serves as the base for shaken summer staples like Margaritas and Palomas, the agave spirit tends to be overlooked when it comes to colder-weather, stirred cocktails. But from smoky Boulevardier riffs to lighter aperitifs, tequila adds earthy and herbaceous dimension to a variety of cozy drinks.

title: This Mesmerizing Garnish Requires No Fancy Tools at All
summary: Giacosa 1815 in Florence, Italy found a clever way to deck out its Cosmo Negroni.
content:
“The moment we start spinning the cocktail, you can see guests’ expressions change,” says Greta Bazzichi, bartender at Giacosa 1815 in Florence, Italy. 

The drink in question is the Cosmo Negroni, created by Bazzichi’s co-worker William Franci in 2024, which is garnished with mesmerizing swirls.

As with so many modern ideas, the concept behind the garnish was sparked while scrolling social media. On his day off, Franci came across videos from an artist—unfortunately he can’t remember the specific account—making designs by carefully layering dyed sand in a bucket before rapidly spinning it. The result was a spiral effect that Franci thought could work well behind the bar. At Giacosa, he grabbed the first two powders he could find, raspberry and cocoa, and used them on a creamy, sour-style cocktail. “The effect was exactly what I had imagined,” he says.

Franci calls the technique “the dust cosmo.” Creating it is simple: it requires applying straight lines of colored powders directly to the foam of a cocktail before spinning the glass. Centrifugal force fans the powders out into a galactic looking pattern (hence “cosmo,” like the cosmos) across the surface. 

In addition to the Cosmo Negroni (which Giacosa makes with cachaça and a raspberry tonka syrup), the bar uses this trick on one of its nonalcoholic serves, the Rossino. Franci says the garnish works on almost any cocktail or coffee drink with a foam, and it’s easy to experiment with it. But there are a few things that make the method easier to execute. First, the foam needs to be dry and airy, or else the powders will stick in place and won’t be able to freely glide across the drink. Second, you need a level surface, so a Whiskey Sour on the rocks or an iced latte won’t work because the powders won’t spread evenly. “The ice moves with the spin of the liquid,” explains Franci, “disrupting the surface and ruining the pattern.”

The other factor that can vary is the speed of the spin. Franci finds that a smooth, slow turn makes the layered swirl he is looking for, but a smaller glass or more fragile foam may require a slower pace. The faster the spin, the looser the pattern. 

After I posted a video of this simple technique, I heard from bartenders and baristas who were abuzz with ideas about how to translate the design onto their own drinks. In an industry where trends can be so cyclical, the novel trick struck a chord. I can’t wait to see dust cosmos topping cocktails and coffee drinks around the world soon.

title: Why You Should be “Densing” Your Daiquiri
summary: In place of fat-washing and traditional emulsion, a new technique from Iain McPherson is already upping other bars’ prep game.
content:
Philip Dizard, who owns Tin’s with his wife Mercury Tin, has always thought of the Daiquiri as “the bartender’s omelette.” It’s “an incredibly simple thing to make, but a remarkably difficult thing to perfect,” says Dizard. “I love that kind of simplicity because it invites an almost endless pursuit of refinement.”

That pursuit led Dizard to a process called “densing,” which he’d been following online. The technique was developed by Iain McPherson, founder of the lauded Panda & Sons in Edinburgh, Scotland. McPherson is known for his mad-science tinkering and innovation; in his bar lab, dubbed the “Brain Melting Society,” he has invented influential techniques like “sous pression,” “switching” and “cryo concentration.”  

Using a vacuum blender to integrate oils into liquids, densing boosts the texture of drinks. McPherson likens the process to emulsification, but without the need for binders or thickeners, and its effects to fat-washing, though this method captures and retains more aromas. 

“When you express citrus oils over [a Martini or Old-Fashioned], that beautiful orange or lemon aroma is incredibly vibrant at first, but it gradually fades as you drink,” he explains. “With densing, we can integrate those oils directly into the spirit, meaning the aroma remains consistent from the first step to the last.” There are also visual results from densing: The process creates “that beautiful louche effect you see when adding water to absinthe or non-chill-filtered whisky,” he says. Incorporating fats like olive oil plays with color, too, softening a bright red Negroni to a pastel peachy pink, for example. It’s an unexpected, but welcome look in a sea of clarified cocktails. 

Here’s how it works: Everything goes into the vacuum blender, which is essentially a blender that removes air while blending; this is typically used to prevent oxidation and create smoother, more consistent textures. McPherson says it’s important to keep all liquids, fat and spirit, around the same temperature—he suggests between 40 and 60 degrees centigrade, or 104 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit—and that using about 0.5 to 2.5 percent fat is the optimal proportion. After a run (or two or three) of the blender, the fat becomes so wholly absorbed into the spirit that they become one inseparable liquid.

McPherson has been an open book with his techniques. “When I saw some of the videos Iain uploaded online,” Dizard recalls, “I sent one to [Tin’s bar director Bowen Kirkwood] and said, ‘What is a vacuum blender and how fast can we get one?’ By the time he responded to my text, I’d already found and bought it.”

The Dako-Ri at Tin’s.

The Dako-Ri is an ode to Dako Tea, a tea shop that Dizard and Tin visited on their honeymoon in Yunnan, China. It specializes in a drink he calls “remarkable” with tea, honey, lemongrass and aromatic local citrus. To capture the memory of that drink in a Daiquiri, Tin’s taps fresh lemongrass in a rum infusion, a syrup made with Mao Jian tea, fresh lime juice and—thanks to densing—olive oil.

Though the Dako-Ri uses a cutting-edge technique, it was important to Dizard to maintain the familiar format of the classic: rum, lime, sugar. “Anything else, and it can be a great drink, but not a Daiquiri,” says Dizard. While he did “take a little bit of liberty,” he stuck close to the script. The lemongrass infusion brings grassiness and extra brightness, and the tea contributes a toasted sticky rice flavor with a hint of savoriness in the finish. The olive oil provides a beautifully rounded texture.

“Some of the best versions of Daiquiris I’ve had skew a little sweeter than they technically should be” in order to get the right mouthfeel, says Dizard. On the other hand, “a lot of contemporary interpretations take it really lean, really acidic, often with an ounce of lime to three-quarters of an ounce of sweeter proportions. We flip that… and in combination with the olive oil emulsion, you get both the upfront [and] the acidity.”

For the Dako-Ri, Dizard pours all the ingredients into the vacuum blender, then reduces the atmospheric pressure inside the chamber, allowing the oil and other ingredients to emulsify. Dizard uses a one-percent olive oil proportion, by weight, in relation to the infused rum. In the vacuum blender, he sets the mix to have three-minute agitations with 30-second rests in between.

Why not just fat-wash the drink? For one, this method maintains the Daiquiri’s acidity. For another, “a fat-wash technique might take 12 to 14 hours, and might leave subtle residue,” Dizard says. Densing, meanwhile, “takes about 15 minutes.” The team can also produce larger batches of cocktails because the vacuum-blender emulsion creates a more stable, not separated, liquid. “I have a pint-glass tester of dense rum that’s been sitting for six months at ambient temperature,” says Dizard. “It hasn’t changed at all.”

A vacuum blender can cost anywhere from $350 to $2,000, but for Dizard, it’s a worthy investment. He says the tool could transform prep for other bar teams. Tin’s not only uses the blender for its densed Dako-Ri, but also to infuse olive oil into mezcal for its El Popular cocktail. “The prep time, refrigerator time and space and labor time saved is remarkable,” says Dizard.

title: A Negroni for Every Mood
summary: Our favorite riffs on the Italian classic, from a mezcal take to a Root Beer Negroni.
content:
As the canonical expression of aperitivo, the Negroni has gained veritable cult status. Built most often (but not always) on an equal-parts formula of gin, sweet vermouth and Campari, this now-ubiquitous template has spurred what seems like an endless number of mutations. 

Whether it’s playing with the ratios or introducing new ingredients to the format—olive brine in a dirty Negroni, for example, or the many mezcal Negronis—these riffs prove that even in a three-ingredient drink, there’s always room for improvement. Here are our favorites.
